panel.noMore: There is no more help for this field.

haFencing.alt: HA diagram: when a node dies, it is cut off (fenced) and its VMs start again on another node.
haFencing.note: Fencing stops a node we think is dead from running the
haFencing.note2: same VM at the same time and corrupting its disk.

backupChain.alt: Backup pool incremental diagram: one full backup, then only what changed (incremental) is chained on. Only when incremental is on; a backup store has no such chain.
backupChain.restore: Restore = full + the increments after it
backupChain.note: In a backup pool, longer chains mean faster, smaller backups but slower restores. A backup store restores each backup on its own.

replicationDr.alt: Replication and DR diagram: VMs at the main site are copied to a standby site on a schedule and started there in a disaster.
replicationDr.note: A shorter schedule means less data lost in a disaster (RPO).
replicationDr.note2: Run a test now and then to check the copies start.

sdn.alt: SDN diagram: VMs on several nodes join one virtual switch; a virtual router sends traffic out with SNAT; a floating IP brings traffic in.
sdn.note: VMs share one private network on any node.

securityGroup.alt: Security group diagram: incoming connections reach the VM only if a rule allows them; outgoing connections are allowed by default.
securityGroup.note: Rules are set separately for incoming and outgoing traffic.
securityGroup.note2: Incoming connections with no matching rule are blocked.

placement.alt: Placement diagram: 'together' keeps VMs on the same node; 'apart' keeps them on different nodes.
placement.note: '(hard)' rules block the start if broken; '(if possible)' rules apply when possible.

storageSharing.alt: Storage diagram: local storage is separate on each node, so moving a VM copies its disk; shared storage is used by all nodes, so only memory moves.
storageSharing.note: HA restarts on another node need the disks on shared storage, or a replica of the local disks on that node.

thinOvercommit.alt: Thin provisioning diagram: three VMs are promised 60 GiB each but the real disk is 100 GiB; each uses only what it writes.
thinOvercommit.promised: Size promised to VMs (180 GiB total)
thinOvercommit.note: Disks use only what they write, so you can promise more than you have.
thinOvercommit.warn: If the real disk fills up, VMs cannot write and pause.

liveMigration.alt: Live migration diagram: the VM keeps running while its memory is copied, changed pages are sent again, then it pauses briefly and continues on the new node.
liveMigration.step1: Send all memory while it runs
liveMigration.step3: Pause very briefly and continue on the new node

declarativeApply.alt: Manage-as-code diagram: 1 the YAML file is 2 compared with the cluster to show what will change, 3 applying makes the cluster match, 4 later changes in the UI show up as 'differs from the file'.
declarativeApply.watch: Drift watch: UI edits show as 'differs from file'
declarativeApply.note: File = wanted state. Apply makes the cluster match.

dedupStore.alt: Backup store diagram: three backups repeat the same pieces, but the store keeps each different piece only once.
dedupStore.note: Identical data is stored once, so many backups take little space.
dedupStore.note2: Clean-up (GC) removes pieces no backup uses.

quorum.alt: Voting diagram: with two of three nodes up there is a majority, so the cluster keeps running.
quorum.note: With 2 nodes, losing one breaks the majority and stops.
quorum.note2: Use 3 or more nodes, or a vote-only node (witness).

page.what: A storage pool tells Orbivisor about one place to keep VM disks. Creating a pool does not wipe or format anything — it uses a folder, volume group, dataset, NFS export or Ceph pool that already exists.
page.how: Local pools (directory, LVM-thin, ZFS) are separate on each node, so moving a VM to another node copies its whole disk. Shared pools (NFS, Ceph RBD, shared LVM, directories marked shared) are seen by every node, so only memory moves.
page.when: With one node or for a test, start with a directory pool. With several nodes that need HA or fast migration, add one shared pool.
page.caution: Deleting a pool keeps its files and images. A pool that still holds volumes, backups, a backup store or OVA exports cannot be deleted.

kind.what: Chooses where and how disks are stored.
kind.how:
Directory: simplest, a folder on the node's disk (qcow2 files — snapshots).
LVM-thin: fast, takes only what is written, snapshots (per node).
ZFS: compression and snapshots (per node).
NFS: a NAS share used by all nodes.
Ceph RBD: distributed storage across several nodes' disks, used by all nodes.
Shared LVM: a SAN (iSCSI/FC) LUN used by all nodes, no snapshots.
kind.when: Start with Directory. With several nodes and a NAS use NFS; with 3+ nodes that each have spare disks use Ceph.
kind.caution: The kind cannot be changed later. VMs on a per-node pool are restarted by HA only on a node that has a replica of their disks.

thinpool.what: A 'thin pool' inside LVM — VM disks are promised a size but only take the space they actually write.
thinpool.how: A VM with a 100 GiB disk that wrote 10 GiB uses only 10 GiB of the thin pool, so you can hand out more than the pool holds (overcommit).
thinpool.caution: If the thin pool fills up, the VMs on it cannot write and pause. Turn on a usage alert.

page.what: A cluster is a group of nodes that share one state. The voters (usually 3, 5 or 7 nodes) vote on changes, so a majority of them must be alive to create or change VMs and to restart HA VMs.
page.how:
Voter: votes and keeps the cluster state. The leader is the voter doing the work right now.
Joining: a new node catching up on the state — when done it becomes a voter only if the voter count (default 5) is not reached; otherwise it stays a read-only member.
Read-only member: follows the state without voting — adding many does not slow the cluster.
Vote-only node (witness): runs no VMs and only votes.
page.when: With 2 nodes, losing 1 breaks the majority (2 of 2 votes) and the cluster stops. Use 3 or more nodes, or add a small vote-only node to a 2-node cluster.
page.caution: An even number of voters does not tolerate more failures (4 nodes still survive only 1). Use 3 or 5.

page.what: A node is one server that runs VMs. This page shows each node's state, resources and failure handling at a glance.
page.how: Maintenance stops placing new VMs on the node, and Drain node moves running VMs to other nodes. HA VMs run only on nodes with a forced-reboot device (watchdog): when a node loses the cluster it first stops its HA VMs, and if that fails the watchdog reboots it, so another node can safely start the same VM.
page.when: Before servicing or updating a server, turn on maintenance and move its VMs off. Labels for placement rules (such as zone=rack-a) are set here too.
page.caution: A live node cannot be removed here. Run orbivisorctl cluster leave on that node.

fence.what: Force-isolating a failed node (fencing) cuts its power so a node that only seemed dead cannot run the same VMs at the same time.
fence.how: When the node stops sending its heartbeat, the leader powers it off through its remote management card (IPMI, Redfish) or a command, and as soon as it is confirmed off starts the VMs on another node. With no method, or if all fail, it waits until the node stops itself (watchdog).
fence.when: Set it up whenever the servers have a BMC (iDRAC, iLO, IPMI). Recovery no longer waits for the node to stop itself (watchdog), so it is faster (about 22 s → about 10 s with the default fast profile; about 62 s → about 30 s with safe), and above all the node is confirmed off first.
fence.caution: Every node must reach the management cards. Use Test first to check the power can be read (it does not change the power).

page.what: A network is what a VM's network card plugs into. When you create or edit a VM you pick one of these networks for each network card.
page.how:
Bridge: plugs into a real bridge on the node, so VMs sit on the same network as your LAN.
VXLAN: joins the nodes with a tunnel so a VM sees the same network on any node.
SDN: a virtual switch spanning the nodes, with address ranges, automatic addresses (DHCP), routers and floating IPs (external addresses).
External (provider): the door from SDN to the real physical network.
page.when: One node, or VMs that should sit right on your LAN: bridge. Several nodes where a VM must keep its network wherever it moves: VXLAN or SDN.
page.caution: Networks used by VMs, routers, floating IPs or load balancers, or with a migration running, cannot be deleted. The user network (QEMU NAT) always exists and is not listed.

kind.what: Chooses how this network is built.
kind.how:
Bridge: plugs into a bridge the node already has (vmbr0 and so on). Simplest. Administrators only.
VXLAN: Orbivisor creates a bridge and a tunnel (UDP 4789) on every node and joins them.
SDN (OVN): a virtual switch spanning the nodes, with subnets, DHCP, routers, floating IPs and security groups. Set up SDN on the SDN screen first.
External (provider): the real physical network SDN routers use to reach the outside. Administrators only.
kind.when: First time: bridge (if you are not an administrator, VXLAN or SDN). A private network across several nodes (with routers and floating IPs): SDN. Just joining the nodes: VXLAN.
kind.caution: The kind cannot change later. Bridge and VXLAN networks can move to SDN later with the simple → SDN migration (⇄ button).

vlan.what: A VLAN tag is a number (1–4094) that splits one switch into separate networks. Only networks with the same number can talk to each other.
vlan.how: Packets from VMs on this network leave with this number attached. Empty sends them without a number (untagged).
vlan.when: Use it when your network team gave you a number, such as 'put VMs on VLAN 20'. If unsure, leave it empty.
vlan.caution: The switch port the node is plugged into must be a trunk (carries several VLANs), and for a bridge network the node's bridge needs VLAN awareness (vlan_filtering 1). Without it, VMs do not start on that node.

physnet.what: A physical network (physnet) is a name given to a node's real network (bridge). It is how SDN reaches the outside.
physnet.how: On the Nodes screen you map 'name → bridge' on each node; here you only pick the name. Bridge names may differ per node.
physnet.when: To reach the internet or your LAN through SDN routers, or to use floating IPs (external addresses), you need one such external network.

mtu.what: The MTU is the largest packet (in bytes) sent at once.
mtu.how: VXLAN and SDN wrap packets in a tunnel, so the default is the physical MTU minus the tunnel header (with 1500: VXLAN 1450, SDN 1442). External (provider) networks have no tunnel, so the default is 1500.
mtu.when: Usually leave it empty. Raise it only when the physical switches take jumbo frames (9000) — even then subtract the tunnel header: VXLAN 8950, SDN 8942.
mtu.caution: Setting it larger than the physical network allows drops big packets, so web pages and file copies seem to hang. An SDN network's MTU cannot change after it is created.

page.what: A backup is a copy of a VM's disks, settings and firmware state at one moment. It stays after the VM is deleted, and you can make a new VM from it (restore) or take out a few files.
page.how: By default every backup copies the whole disk (full). With incremental on, a backup pool copies only what changed since the previous backup and chains them; a restore reads the full one and each later one in turn. A backup store has no chain — it reads only changed pieces, but every backup has a complete list, so any backup is restored or deleted on its own.
page.when: For one backup now, use 'Back up now' on the VM. For daily backups, create a backup schedule.
page.caution: Backups on the same disk are lost with that disk. Keep them on another disk, a NAS or a remote cluster too.

target.what: What kind of place keeps the backup.
target.how:
Backup pool: one whole file per disk. Easy and simple.
Backup store: disks are cut into pieces and each identical piece is kept once. Saves a lot of space with many VMs, and offers encryption, verification and S3.
target.when: With a few VMs a backup pool is enough. With many VMs, or when you need S3 or encryption, use a backup store.

incremental.what: A backup that copies only what changed since the previous one. Off by default (every backup is full).
incremental.how:
Backup pool: incrementals follow one full backup in a chain. They are fast and small, but a restore reads the full backup and every incremental after it.
Backup store: only changed pieces are read, so it is fast, but there is no chain. Every backup has a complete list and restores on its own.
incremental.when: Turn it on for large VMs that are backed up often.
incremental.caution: When the VM is stopped or there is no earlier backup, a full backup is taken. The Type column shows why.

page.what: A backup schedule says when to back up which VMs, where, and how many backups to keep.
page.how: At the set time (UTC) the cluster backs up the chosen VMs one after another, then deletes backups older than the retention rules. It can also send copies to a remote cluster or another store.
page.when: Once a night is usual for production VMs. Turn on remote replication for important ones.
page.caution: Each node runs only a few backups at once, so many VMs make a run take longer.

retention.what: How many backups to keep and for how long, counted per VM.
retention.how:
Last: the n newest backups.
Daily: the newest one per day, for n days that have one.
Weekly: one per week, for n weeks.
Monthly: one per month, for n months.
Backups made by this schedule that no rule keeps are deleted (except ones a kept incremental still needs). Manual 'Back up now' backups and other schedules' backups are never deleted.
retention.when: Last 3, Daily 7, Weekly 4, Monthly 3 lets you go back three months.
retention.caution: All 0 deletes no successful backup, so space keeps growing. A failed backup is deleted once a later one succeeds.

fullEvery.what: How many incremental backups (reading only the changes) before a full one again. The default 0 means always full.
fullEvery.how:
Backup pool: with 6 it repeats 'one full + six of only the changes'. With daily backups that is one full and six incremental a week.
Backup store: with 6, after six backups that read only changed pieces, the next one reads the whole disk again. Space and restore time do not change.
fullEvery.when: In a backup pool, larger is faster and smaller, but a restore reads more pieces. If you use incrementals, 6 is usual for daily backups.

page.what: Settings that apply to the whole cluster. Change a section and press its Save; it reaches every node at once.
page.how:
Updates: the channel nodes get packages from.
Host shutdown and HA: what happens to VMs when a node is shut down or dies.
CPU baseline: makes VMs see the same CPU on every node (so moving them never breaks them).
Usage reports: a daily report with versions, counts and totals only (no names or addresses).
Prometheus: the address an external metrics server reads.
page.when: Look through it once after installing, and when you change the update policy or monitoring.

channel.what: The repository nodes get Orbivisor packages from.
channel.how:
Stable: only proven versions.
Testing: new versions first — good for a test cluster.
Enterprise: the subscribers' repository; needs a subscription key.
channel.when: Use stable or enterprise for production.
channel.caution: Changing the channel does not update anything yet. Apply updates per node from the Nodes page.

telemetry.what: A short usage report that tells the developers how many clusters run which versions.
telemetry.how: Once a day the leader node sends versions, counts (nodes, VMs, pools and networks by type, …), total CPUs and memory, and the subscription level. You see the exact report before turning it on. A new report ID breaks the link to earlier reports.
telemetry.when: Turn it on to help improve the product. Everything works the same when it is off.
telemetry.caution: No names, IPs, keys or VM contents are sent.

prometheus.what: Prometheus is a common monitoring tool that collects server metrics for graphs and alerts. Turning this on opens a metrics URL on every node.
prometheus.how: Prometheus reads each node's metrics URL at a fixed interval (scrape). Each node exports only its own node, VMs and pools, so add every node as a target. It needs an API token of a viewer or higher.
prometheus.when: Turn it on if you already watch other servers with Prometheus or Grafana. Not needed if you only use this UI's metrics and alerts.
prometheus.example: Paste the example below into scrape_configs in prometheus.yml and put an API token in the token field.

haReserve.what: Keeps memory free on the other nodes to take a dead node's HA VMs.
haReserve.how:
None: nothing is kept free (recovery may run out of room).
Number of nodes: memory worth n nodes, starting with the largest, is kept free.
Percent of memory: n% of all memory is kept free.
Starting an HA VM that would use this room is refused.
haReserve.when: Choose one node's worth so every HA VM can start again when any one node dies.
haReserve.example: 3 nodes of 128 GiB, one node's worth → running VMs, HA or not, may use up to 256 GiB in all
haReserve.caution: All running VMs count, HA or not. Migrations are not blocked.

haConcurrency.what: How many VMs one node starts at once during HA recovery.
haConcurrency.how: Each node that takes the dead node's VMs starts this many at a time, and the next when one finishes.
haConcurrency.when: Raise it with fast storage; lower it when recovery slows down from disk and CPU spikes. Default 4.
haConcurrency.caution: Too high makes disk and CPU load jump during recovery and slows every VM.

shutdownPolicy.what: What happens to a node's HA VMs when the node reboots or powers off.
shutdownPolicy.how:
🔄 Reboot: VMs pause → start again on the same node when it returns
⏻ Power off: start on another node
Conditional (default) pauses on reboot and starts elsewhere on power off. 'Move first' moves the VMs to other nodes while running before shutting down.
shutdownPolicy.when: Usually Conditional. Choose 'Move first' if VMs must not stop even for update reboots.
shutdownPolicy.caution: It does not apply when only orbivisord stops or is upgraded; the VMs keep running then.

page.what: A subscription gives access to the enterprise update channel and support. The key holds the customer name, level, node count and expiry date.
page.how: The key applies to the whole cluster. When there are more nodes than the key allows, or it expires, its state changes and the enterprise channel stops giving updates.
page.when: Paste the key you received after buying a subscription. Every feature works without one.

page.what: SDN (software-defined networking) builds virtual switches and virtual routers across the nodes. A VM keeps the same private network and address wherever it moves. Similar to VMware NSX.
page.how:
Orbivisor installs and runs OVN (Open Virtual Network).
Central nodes (1, 3 or 5): run the databases that store the settings (NB, SB) and northd, which translates them. SDN keeps working while a majority is alive.
Node connectors (chassis, ovn-controller): run on every node with VMs and join the nodes with tunnels (Geneve).
On top you create SDN networks (virtual switches), routers, floating IPs (external addresses) and security groups.
page.when: Use it when you have several nodes and need one private network wherever a VM runs, or want private VMs to reach the internet through a router or be reached from outside through a floating IP. With one node, or when plugging into your LAN is enough, a bridge network will do.
page.caution: 2 or 4 central nodes survive no more failures than 1 or 3. Three is recommended.

chassis.what: A chassis is the OVN connector program (ovn-controller) on each node. It takes the settings from the central nodes and builds that node's VM ports and the tunnels between nodes.
chassis.how: Ready means SDN VMs can start on that node. The Geneve address is the one the node uses for tunnels to the others.
chassis.when: After adding a node to the cluster, press Install here so SDN VMs can run on it too.
chassis.caution: SDN VMs on a node marked down may have lost their network.

centrals.what: Central nodes store all SDN settings (switches, routers, addresses, rules) and hand them out to the nodes.
centrals.how: The settings live in two databases (northbound NB, southbound SB) replicated between the central nodes (Raft); northd translates NB into SB. A majority of central nodes must be alive to change settings; without it, running VMs keep their network.
centrals.when: Start with 3 (one can fail). To replace a node, add the new central node first, then remove the old one.
centrals.caution: 2 or 4 are no better than 1 or 3 (a majority is harder to reach).

address.what: The address other nodes use to reach the databases on the first central node.
address.how: Empty uses the node's address. If the node has several networks (management, storage), pick the one the nodes reach each other on.
address.caution: Loopback (127.0.0.1) and link-local (169.254.x, fe80::) addresses are not allowed.

subnet.what: A subnet is the range of IP addresses used on this network, written as a CIDR.
subnet.how: /24 is 256 addresses (about 250 for VMs), /16 is 65536. Orbivisor picks a unique address for each VM and hands it out with DHCP.
subnet.when: Each network takes one IPv4 and one IPv6 subnet at most. Pick a range that does not overlap other networks or your LAN.
subnet.caution: The range and gateway cannot change once saved. A subnet can be removed only when no VM, router, floating IP or load balancer uses it and no migration is running.

ipv6Mode.what: How VMs get an IPv6 address.
ipv6Mode.how:
None: set inside the VM (or by first-boot setup).
SLAAC: VMs build their own address from router advertisements (RA).
DHCPv6 (stateful): a DHCP server assigns the address.
SLAAC + DHCPv6 (stateless): the address from SLAAC, extras such as DNS from DHCPv6.
ipv6Mode.caution: SLAAC modes need a /64 subnet, and advertisements go out only while this network is attached to a router. It cannot change while VMs hold addresses in this subnet (their addresses would change).

dhcp.what: DHCP lets a VM get its address, gateway and DNS automatically when it starts.
dhcp.how: SDN's built-in DHCP hands out the address Orbivisor picked for each VM. No separate DHCP server is needed.
dhcp.when: On SDN networks, usually leave it on. Turn it off only to enter the address inside the VM yourself — even then use the address Orbivisor assigned (other addresses, or ones from another DHCP server, are blocked). External (provider) networks have it off by default, and DHCP gives IPv4 only.

gateway.what: A gateway node actually hosts a router's external gateway. SNAT (private VMs going out) passes through it. Floating IP traffic leaves straight from the VM's node when that node has the physical network, and goes through the gateway node only when it does not.
gateway.how: Among gateway candidates with the external network's physical network ready, the highest priority hosts it; if it fails the next takes over within seconds (BFD).
gateway.when: Turn it on only on nodes plugged into the outside network (internet line, LAN). With two or more, the outside stays reachable when one fails.
gateway.caution: Open SNAT connections are cut during a takeover.

range.what: Floating IP ranges are the addresses on the external network handed out as router outside addresses and floating IPs (external addresses).
range.how: When a router attaches to the external network it takes one address from here for SNAT (private VMs going out). Each floating IP you create takes one from here and is tied to one VM.
range.when: Enter the block of addresses your company or data center gave you for this network. If empty, the allocation ranges are used.
range.caution: Overlapping addresses used by DHCP or other devices causes address conflicts.

page.what: A floating IP (external address) maps one address of an external network 1:1 to one interface of a private VM. Any address on the external network works, even a private range (such as 192.168.x.x) — it does not have to be an internet address. The CLI and API name is floating IP too (orbivisorctl fip).
page.how:
Traffic from outside to the external address (such as 203.0.113.120) is handed to the VM's private address (such as 10.10.0.5) by the router, and the VM goes out with the external address. Nothing changes inside the VM. You can detach it and attach it to another VM, so the address survives a server swap.
Distributed: leaves straight from the VM's node. Centralized: goes through the gateway node.
page.when: When the outside must reach a VM first, like a web server or VPN. For going out only, the router's SNAT is enough. To spread traffic over several VMs, use a load balancer.
page.caution: The VM's network must be attached to a router that goes out to that external network. A security group blocking inbound traffic stops it too. It counts toward the folder's floating IP quota.

nic.what: The VM network card to attach this floating IP to.
nic.how: Each card takes one floating IP. Cards you cannot pick show why (no router, no IPv4, already attached).
nic.when: You can also create it unattached and use Attach in the list later.

page.what: Gets public HTTPS certificates automatically, so the browser shows a padlock without warnings. ACME is the standard for ordering and renewing certificates automatically; Let's Encrypt is the most common certificate authority that gives free certificates with it.
page.how:
1. ACME account: registers this cluster with the certificate authority (the server makes the key).
2. Certificate: list the domains; the leader orders within a minute, proves domain ownership and gets the certificate.
3. Every node swaps in the new certificate without restarting. It renews automatically before expiry.
page.when: Use it when users reach this UI by a domain name (such as vm.example.com). If they only use IP addresses, importing the cluster CA into the browser is simpler.
page.caution: The domain must point at these nodes, and for HTTP-01 each node's port 80 must be reachable from the internet. Use Let's Encrypt staging while testing (production has weekly rate limits).

directory.what: The ACME address of the certificate authority (CA) that issues certificates.
directory.how:
Let's Encrypt: free, 90-day certificates, the most common.
Let's Encrypt (staging): for testing — browsers do not trust it, but there are no rate limits.
ZeroSSL, Google Trust Services: free, need an EAB key.
Other ACME directory: enter the address of an in-house CA such as step-ca.
directory.when: First try staging once; when it works, add a Let's Encrypt account.

challenge.what: How the certificate authority checks that the domain is really yours.
challenge.how:
HTTP-01: the CA reads http://<domain>/.well-known/…, so each node's port 80 must be reachable from the internet.
DNS-01: writes a temporary TXT record in the domain's DNS. No open port needed, and wildcards (*.example.com) work — add a DNS provider first.
challenge.when: HTTP-01 when nodes are open to the internet; DNS-01 for private networks or wildcards.

scope.what: Whether all nodes share one certificate or each node gets its own.
scope.how:
Shared: one certificate installed on every node (for example api.example.com behind a load balancer).
Per node: {node} in a name becomes the node name and each node gets its own (for example {node}.example.com → node-a.example.com).
scope.when: Shared when users come in by one name; per node when they use each node's own address.

eab.what: External account binding (EAB) is a key pair (key id + HMAC key) that links the account you made on the CA's website to this ACME account.
eab.when: ZeroSSL, Google Trust Services and many in-house CAs require it. Let's Encrypt does not.
eab.caution: The HMAC key is not shown again after saving.

page.what: A backup store keeps identical content only once. VM disks are cut into 4 MiB pieces and a piece already in the store is not written again.
page.how: Ten VMs with the same OS keep the OS pieces only once. Each backup lists the pieces it uses, so any backup can be restored or deleted on its own. Space cleanup removes pieces no backup uses and gives the space back.
page.when: Use a store with many VMs, to keep backups in S3, or to encrypt on the nodes. With a few VMs a backup pool is enough.
page.caution: Deleting backups frees space only at the next cleanup. An encrypted store opens with either its recovery key or its escrow passphrase — lose both and the backups cannot be opened.

backend.what: Where the pieces are actually kept.
backend.how:
Backup pool: a store/<id> folder inside a directory or NFS pool of the nodes.
S3-compatible: a bucket on AWS S3, MinIO, Ceph RGW and similar — good for keeping backups off site.
backend.when: A NAS in the same building: backup pool. Somewhere else: S3.

encryption.what: Whether backups are encrypted before they leave the node.
encryption.how:
No encryption: compression only.
Encrypt with a new key: makes a new key and shows the recovery key (OPK1-…) once.
Use a recovery key: opens with the same key as another store (to receive remote copies).
Open with an escrow passphrase: opens with the key wrapped by a passphrase inside the store.
encryption.when: Encrypt when the store is in S3 or on equipment someone else runs.
encryption.caution: Losing both the recovery key and the passphrase means the backups cannot be recovered. It cannot be changed later.

gc.what: Space cleanup (GC) removes pieces no backup uses and gives the space back.
gc.how: It marks the pieces in use, waits for running backups to finish, then removes the unmarked pieces.
gc.when: Once a day after the backups finish (such as 05:00 UTC) is usual.
gc.caution: Deleting backups frees space only after a cleanup runs.

page.what: The official cloud images of distributions such as Ubuntu, Debian and Rocky — disks that boot straight away with no installer.
page.how: Download makes a node that can use the pool fetch the image from the publisher, check it against the publisher's checksum and keep it as a disk (volume). With 'Create a template after downloading' on, a stopped template VM is also made from that disk.
page.when: Use it to create many Linux VMs quickly: make one template, then clone it when creating VMs.
page.caution: The downloading node must reach the internet (the publisher). Removing an entry from the list keeps disks and templates already downloaded.

makeTemplate.what: Makes a 'template VM' from the downloaded disk — a VM you never start and only clone from.
makeTemplate.how: After the download the disk is grown to the size you give, and a stopped VM is made with one network card and first-boot setup (user, password, SSH keys).
makeTemplate.when: Turn it on when you will create several VMs of this OS. For a single VM you can just download the disk.
makeTemplate.caution: If making the template fails, the downloaded disk is kept. You can make the template again from Templates.

diskSize.what: The disk size of the template (and of VMs cloned from it).
diskSize.how: Cloud images come small (built-in images are about 2–10 GiB — for example Ubuntu 24.04 3.5 GiB, Rocky 9 10 GiB). The disk is grown to the size you give, and the guest widens its partition on first boot. A qcow2 disk does not take the promised size at once — only what is written.
diskSize.example: 20 → a 20 GiB disk (actually using a few GiB at first)
diskSize.caution: It cannot be smaller than the image, and later it can only grow, never shrink.

checksum.what: How to check that the downloaded image is not broken or tampered with.
checksum.how:
Checksum file: give the address of the publisher's file such as SHA256SUMS; the node finds this image's hash in it (keeps working when the release changes).
SHA-256 / SHA-512: write the hash itself. When the image changes, the value must be written again.
checksum.when: When the publisher offers a checksum file, it is the easiest.

page.what: ISO files (installer CD images) for installing operating systems.
page.how: An upload goes to the node you are connected to; a URL download is fetched by a node that uses the pool. Put the ISO in a VM's CD-ROM and boot to start the installer. Many VMs can have the same ISO at once.
page.when: For Windows or an OS without a cloud image. For Linux, OS images (cloud images) are faster.
page.caution: ISOs live only in directory and NFS pools. A VM with an ISO from a node-local pool starts only on that node. An ISO in a VM's drive cannot be deleted.

page.what: Moves VMs you ran on VMware (ESXi, vCenter, Workstation) into Orbivisor VMs.
page.how: Upload an OVA file or connect to ESXi and pick a VM: its CPU, memory, disks and networks are read and settings are proposed. Review them and press Import to convert the disks and create a stopped VM.
page.when: For a few VMs at a time. To move dozens while they keep running, use VMware migration (warm migration).
page.caution: The source VM must be powered off. Power off the VMware original before you start the imported VM, so the same address never comes up twice.

devices.what: Which virtual devices the imported VM's disks and network cards use.
devices.how:
Import suggests devices from the source OS: SATA and e1000e for Windows, virtio for others.
virtio (virtio-blk): the fast virtual device. The guest needs its drivers (most Linux includes them; Windows needs them installed).
SATA / e1000e: compatible devices. Windows recognises them without drivers, but they are slower.
devices.when: If a Windows VM has no virtio drivers, import it with SATA and e1000e first, install the drivers, then switch to virtio.
devices.caution: Switching to a device without drivers leaves the OS unable to find its disk, so it does not boot.

page.what: The disks (volumes) VMs use. One volume is one disk of a VM.
page.how: A volume is a file or block device inside a storage pool. Volumes in a local pool exist on that node only; volumes in a shared pool are seen by every node. A volume with a 'Clone source (template)' is a linked clone that keeps only its changes on top of a template's disk — flattening makes it stand alone.
page.when: To add another disk to a VM, bring an image file in as a disk, or grow a disk.
page.caution: Deleting a volume erases all its data. A volume attached to a VM must be removed from the VM first.

format.what: How the disk is kept in the pool.
format.how:
qcow2: a file that takes only what is written. Supports snapshots and linked clones.
raw: one plain file the full size of the disk. Fewer features, a little faster.
format.when: Usually keep qcow2 (the default). Use raw when disk speed matters a lot, as for a database, and snapshots are not needed.
format.caution: LVM-thin, ZFS, Ceph and shared LVM pools have no choice: always raw (LVM-thin, ZFS and Ceph do the snapshots themselves; shared LVM has none).

size.what: The disk size promised to the VM.
size.how: On qcow2 and thin pools the promised size is not taken at once — only what is written. So the total handed out can exceed the pool (handing out more than there is).
size.example: A 100 GiB disk with 10 GiB written uses only 10 GiB of the pool.
size.caution: If the total handed out exceeds the pool, the pool can fill up when VMs really write, and the VMs pause. Sizes can only grow.

page.what: The vCenter and ESXi connections Orbivisor reads VMs from.
page.how: Save the address, user and password once, and VMware migration can browse its inventory (the VM list) and let you pick VMs. On the first connection the server's certificate fingerprint is shown, and the password is sent only after you trust it.
page.when: Add a connection here before you move several VMs from VMware.
page.caution: Passwords stay in the cluster and are never shown again. A connection used by a migration cannot be deleted. Free ESXi is read only, so only cold migration works.

vddk.what: Whether disks are read with VMware's disk tool (VDDK).
vddk.how: Off: datastore files are read over HTTPS (enough in most cases). On: disks are read with VDDK, the only way for vSAN and vVols datastores.
vddk.when: Turn it on only when the source VMs are on vSAN or vVols.
vddk.caution: An operator must first install nbdkit and VMware VDDK on every node.

page.what: Moves many VMware VMs to Orbivisor as one plan.
page.how: In the wizard pick a connection (vCenter or ESXi) and VMs, map their networks and datastores to Orbivisor networks and pools once, then start. A warm migration copies VMs while they run and keeps syncing changes, so they are off only briefly at cutover.
page.when: For many VMs, or VMs that cannot be off for long. For a few at a time, Imports (OVA, ESXi) is simpler.
page.caution: Source VMs are never deleted. A cut-over VM can be reverted until you finalize it.

mode.what: Whether VMs move while running or powered off.
mode.how:
Warm: the disks are copied while the source runs, and changed blocks are copied again on a schedule. At cutover the source is shut down and only the last changes are copied, so downtime is short.
Cold: powered-off VMs are copied once. Running VMs are refused.
mode.when: Warm for VMs in service; cold for VMs that can be off, or for free ESXi.
mode.caution: Warm migration keeps a snapshot and change tracking (CBT) on the source. Left for long, the source datastore grows, so do not drag it out.

devices.what: How the disk and network card types of moved VMs are chosen.
devices.how:
By guest OS: Linux gets the fast virtual devices (virtio); Windows, which may lack drivers, gets the compatible devices (SATA, e1000e).
The same for every VM: the types chosen below are used for all VMs.
devices.when: Usually keep 'By guest OS'. If your Windows VMs already have virtio drivers, choose 'The same for every VM' with virtio.

maxFinalDelta.what: A limit on the last changes copied right before cutover.
maxFinalDelta.how: At cutover the last changes are copied while the source is off, so a large amount means long downtime. Over the limit, cutover stops before the source is touched and syncing continues.
maxFinalDelta.example: 5 → no cutover while the last changes exceed 5 GiB
maxFinalDelta.when: Set it when some VMs must keep downtime short. Empty means no limit.

folders.what: Which Orbivisor folder the moved VMs go in.
folders.how:
Put all VMs in one folder: all go in the folder chosen below.
Recreate the VMware folders: vCenter's folder tree is rebuilt under the chosen folder.
folders.when: If you split permissions by folder, recreating the VMware folders keeps things tidy.

page.what: Orbivisor VMs turned into OVA files that VMware (vSphere, Workstation) or VirtualBox can open.
page.how: Choose 'Export as OVA' in a stopped VM's menu; its disks are converted to VMware's format and written to a pool. When done, download it here as one OVA.
page.when: To move a VM to another virtualization product, keep it as a file or hand it to someone. For safekeeping, backups fit better.
page.caution: The VM must stay off while it is written. Deleting an export keeps the VM.

hwVersion.what: The virtual hardware version the receiving VMware product understands.
hwVersion.how: Higher numbers allow newer features, but older ESXi cannot open them. 14 needs ESXi 6.7 or later, 19 needs 7.0 U2, 21 needs 8.0 U2.
hwVersion.when: If you do not know the receiving ESXi version, keep it low (14).

page.what: Ceph is distributed storage that joins the disks of several nodes into one big shared storage. Orbivisor installs and runs it on the nodes itself.
page.how: Three nodes each give empty disks (Ceph disks, OSDs). Ceph splits data into pieces and keeps 3 copies on different nodes. Every node's VMs use the pool built on top, so when a node fails the data survives and VMs can start on another node. Monitors (3 recommended) vote on who is alive; managers collect status.
page.when: With 3 or more nodes that have spare disks and no NAS or SAN. If you already have a Ceph cluster, create a Ceph RBD pool under Storage pools instead.
page.caution: Disks chosen as Ceph disks are wiped entirely. Every node needs the same Ceph release, synchronised clocks (NTP) and open ports (3300, 6789, 6800–7300/tcp).

mon.what: Monitors are the voting members that keep Ceph's map (who is alive, where data is).
mon.how: Ceph reads and writes only while a majority of monitors reach each other. Three survive one down, five survive two. Two monitors cannot lose any, so they are no better than one.
mon.when: Keep three on different nodes. With five or more nodes and a need for more resilience, five.
mon.caution: An even number gains nothing. A node can have only one monitor.

osd.what: A Ceph disk (OSD) is one disk given to Ceph plus the program that looks after it.
osd.how: The chosen disk is wiped entirely and becomes Ceph storage. Ceph spreads data over many Ceph disks and keeps copies on different nodes.
osd.when: Add one or more empty disks of similar size on each node. Three copies need Ceph disks on at least three nodes.
osd.caution: All data on the disk is erased. The OS disk and disks in use cannot be chosen.

poolSize.what: How many copies of each piece of data are kept.
poolSize.how: Copies are always on different nodes. With 3, everything keeps working when one node fails; with two failed nodes the data survives but reads and writes stop until one comes back. Usable space is a third of the total.
poolSize.when: 3 is recommended. 2 with two nodes; 1 only for a single test node.
poolSize.caution: With 1, a single failed disk loses data. With 2, data can be lost while one copy is down.

networks.how:
Public network: where VMs (clients) and monitors reach Ceph.
Cluster network (optional): where Ceph disks copy data to each other. Kept apart, recovery and rebalancing traffic does not get in the way of VM traffic.
networks.when: If the nodes have a separate storage LAN of 10 GbE or more, give it as the cluster network.

page.what: A router is a virtual router joining SDN networks (virtual switches) to each other and private networks to the outside.
page.how:
Attach an SDN network as a router interface and its subnet gateway address becomes the router's address. Pick an external network and the router takes one outside address there, replacing private VMs' addresses with it on the way out (SNAT). To let the outside reach a VM, attach a floating IP (external address).
One gateway node hosts the outside door; if it fails, the next node takes over.
page.when: When private VMs must reach the internet, when two or more SDN networks must talk, or to use floating IPs.
page.caution: A router with interfaces left cannot be deleted. An external network needs a gateway node with that physical network, set on the Nodes screen.

external.what: The external network is the real physical network the router uses to reach the outside (your LAN, the internet). Create it on the Networks screen as External (provider).
external.how: The router takes one outside address from this network's floating IP ranges. The default route (0.0.0.0/0) goes to this network's gateway.
external.when: Pick one for VMs to reach the internet or to use floating IPs. None if the router only joins SDN networks.
external.caution: Changing it changes the outside address. Detach floating IPs going through this router first, and turn off the external VIP of (or delete) load balancers that use it.

snat.what: SNAT (source address translation) replaces the source address of private VMs going out with the router's one outside address (IPv4 only), like a home router.
snat.how: When VM 10.10.0.5 opens a website, the site sees the router's outside address (such as 203.0.113.10). Replies come back through the router to the VM.
snat.when: Usually on. Turn it off only when the outside router knows the private addresses and has routes to them.
snat.caution: SNAT alone does not let the outside reach a VM first; floating IPs or load balancers do that.

routes.what: A static route is a rule like 'send this address range to that device'.
routes.how: The router sends traffic matching a route to its next hop, and everything else to the external network's gateway. Without an external network, traffic with no matching route is dropped.
routes.when: Use it when another network sits behind a VPN or firewall VM inside a private network.
routes.caution: The default route (0.0.0.0/0) comes with the external network; adding it yourself is refused.

page.what: A remote cluster is another Orbivisor cluster in another building or region. This cluster can see its status and send backup copies there. A DR plan lives on the recovering side (the standby site): register the main site as a remote there, and its VMs' copies are brought back up on that cluster.
page.how: Register it with its address, CA fingerprint and an API token made there. Its status is collected every 30 seconds. Turning on remote replication in a backup schedule sends a copy of each backup to a pool or store there.
page.when: When work must go on even if one site stops completely from fire, power loss or ransomware.
page.caution: The token's user role decides what can be done there. Do not give it more than needed.

token.what: The key the remote cluster uses to recognise this cluster.
token.how: Create it under Settings › API tokens on the remote cluster. This cluster can do there only what that token's user may do.
token.when: For backup copies only, use a user that can write backups. When a standby site registers the main site for DR, the token (made on the main site) needs to read VMs and backups, stop and start VMs, and create and send backups there (the standby site restores VMs itself).
token.caution: The token is not shown again. Enter it again when the address or CA changes.

page.what: A DR (disaster recovery) plan is the running order for starting a production site's VMs on this cluster when that whole site is lost.
page.how:
The production cluster keeps sending backup copies here (remote replication). A failover goes through the boot groups in order: for each group it restores the VMs from the newest copies (networks and IPs changed to suit this site) and starts them. The next group's restore begins after the previous group finishes.
Test: starts them on test networks that cannot reach production, then cleans up.
Planned migration: stops the production VMs and moves up to a last backup (no data lost).
Disaster failover: when production is already down, starts from the newest copies.
page.when: Test about once a month and note how long it takes (RTO).
page.caution: After a disaster failover, the same VM may run in both places once production comes back. Make sure the production VMs are stopped (fenced).

source.what: The production cluster the VMs run on now.
source.how: It must be registered as a remote cluster and send backup copies here (remote replication of a backup schedule).

rpo.what: RPO is the most data, in time, you can afford to lose in a disaster.
rpo.how: The age of each VM's newest copy is measured and an alert fires when it is older than the target. The bar shows how close it is to the target.
rpo.when: A copy's age counts from when the backup was made on the main site. Set the target a little above the backup interval plus backup and copy time. With one copy a day, 26 to 30 hours.
rpo.example: RPO 28 hours, backup daily at 03:00: each 03:00 copy normally arrives that morning, so no alert; if a day is missed, the alert fires at 07:00 the next day

groups.what: Boot groups are the order VMs start in.
groups.how: Group 1's VMs are restored and started; when all have finished (ready, failed or timed out), group 2 begins. VMs in a group run together, up to 4 at once (2 per node; setting max_parallel). Whether a timeout stops the run or continues follows the group setting (continue by default).
groups.example: Group 1: db → Group 2: app → Group 3: web
groups.when: Put VMs that depend on others (app → database) in later groups.

wait.what: The condition for moving on to the next group.
wait.how:
VM running: the VM is powered on.
Guest agent answers: the OS is up and its guest agent replies.
Guest reports its IP: the network is up too (the surest).
wait.caution: VMs without a guest agent can only use 'VM running'.

page.what: The progress of one DR run (test, planned migration, disaster failover or cleanup).
page.how: For each VM the step dots fill in order — Restoring → Starting → Waiting → Ready (cleanup: Deleting → Deleted). Each group starts once the group before has finished (ready, failed or timed out). The elapsed time is the RTO.
page.when: When the stalled banner appears, read the task errors below. Cancelling is advised only for a planned migration you can run again — cancelling a failover can leave VMs running on neither side.
page.caution: Always clean up after a test, or the test VMs keep using resources.

page.what: Alerts watch the cluster for you and tell you when something goes wrong.
page.how:
1. Rule: what to watch (for example node CPU > 90% for 5 minutes).
2. While the rule's condition lasts, the alert goes from pending to firing.
3. When it fires, it is sent to the rule's notification targets (email, Slack…); when it clears, that is sent too.
Notifications sent shows what was actually sent and why sending failed.
page.when: After installing, create one notification target and a few basic rules (node offline, pool usage, backup failed).
page.caution: Without a notification target, alerts only show on this page and go nowhere.

condition.what: The kind of condition that fires the alert.
condition.how:
Metric: a node or VM value such as CPU, memory or disk goes above or below a threshold.
Storage pool usage: a pool is fuller than a percentage.
States: something that lasts, such as a node being down or a VM failed — can have a duration.
Events: something that happens once — a task fails, HA recovers, a backup schedule fails, a DR run fails — notified once, right away, with no duration.
Pick the SDN, backup store and DR groups only if you use those features.
condition.example: Node metric · CPU % · above · 90 · for 300 s → notify when CPU stays above 90% for over 5 minutes.

forSecs.what: The condition must last this long before the alert fires. Until then the alert is pending.
forSecs.when: For values that spike, such as CPU, use 60–300 s to avoid noise. For things you must know at once, such as a node going down, use 0–60 s.
forSecs.caution: Too long and you learn about real problems late.

repeatSecs.what: While the alert stays, the same notification is sent again at this interval.
repeatSecs.when: 0 sends only once. For critical alerts you must not miss, use something like 3600 (1 hour).
repeatSecs.caution: A short interval floods the target with the same notification.

severity.what: How serious the alert is. It shows in the colour on screen and in the notification title.
severity.how:
Critical: the service stopped or is about to — fix now.
Warning: fine for now, but a problem if left.
Info: good to know.
severity.when: To send severities to different places, use separate rules and targets.

sendResolved.what: Whether to send one more 'resolved' notice when the problem clears.
sendResolved.how: On (default): a resolved notice is sent when a state condition is back to normal. Events (one-off things such as a task failing or an HA recovery) have nothing to clear, so none is sent.
sendResolved.when: Usually keep it on. Turn it off if there are too many notices.

page.what: A notification target is one place that receives alert notifications, such as a set of email addresses or one Slack channel.
page.how: When an alert rule chooses a target by name, notifications go there when the alert fires and clears. Test sends one test notification right away. Passwords, tokens, header values and the path of a webhook URL are not shown again after saving.
page.when: Create one first when you set up alerts. Make several if teams receive in different places.

kind.how:
Email (SMTP): sends through your mail server.
Webhook: sends an HTTP POST to one address. Choosing Slack, Teams, ntfy or Gotify as the format shapes it for that app.
kind.when: Webhook if you use a chat app, otherwise email.

format.what: The shape of the webhook message.
format.how:
Webhook (JSON): the alert as JSON — for your own server.
Slack, Microsoft Teams: use that app's incoming webhook URL.
ntfy, Gotify: push notification servers for phones — may need a token.

page.what: A security group is a bundle of firewall rules you put on VM network cards. One group (such as web) can go on many VMs, and changing it applies to all of them right away.
page.how:
A card with groups drops new incoming connections by default and accepts only what matches an 'in · accept' rule. Outgoing traffic is sent by default and dropped only when it matches an 'out · drop' rule. Replies to allowed traffic, ARP and DHCP replies always pass.
On simple network cards the node's nftables applies it; on SDN cards OVN ACLs do, with the same order and defaults. Differences: on SDN cards, removing an allow rule also cuts connections already open. Spoofing protection is separate from groups: simple cards block other MAC addresses; SDN cards always block other MAC and IP addresses, even without a group.
page.when: When a VM should open only the ports it needs (for example 443 for a web server, SSH only from the office).
page.caution: A card whose groups have no rules drops all incoming traffic, SSH included. Groups used by VM cards cannot be deleted.

rules.what: A rule says 'accept (or drop) traffic in this direction, with this protocol and port, from or to these addresses'.
rules.how:
Direction: in (to the VM) or out (from the VM).
Action: accept or drop.
Protocol: TCP, UDP, ICMP (IPv4), ICMPv6 or any.
Ports: one such as 22, or a range such as 8000-8080. Empty means all ports.
Remote address: the other side's address range (CIDR). Empty means anywhere.
Rules are checked from the top and the first match decides; reorder them with the arrows.
rules.when: Web server: in · accept · TCP · 443. SSH from the office only: in · accept · TCP · 22 · 203.0.113.0/24.
rules.example:
in accept TCP 22 10.0.0.0/8
in accept TCP 443 (anywhere)
out drop TCP 25 (block sending mail)
rules.caution: A broad drop rule placed above an accept rule makes the accept rule unreachable.

page.what: A virtual machine (VM) is a computer running on a node. This screen lists every VM in the cluster with its state (running, stopped, moving).
page.how: Click a row for the detail screen (summary, console, snapshots, backups). Select several VMs to start, stop or move them to a folder together. The views at the top (running, failed, this node) filter quickly.
page.when: Use Create for a one-off server; deploy from a template when you need several with the same setup.

hotplug.what: Adding disks or network devices without turning the VM off.
hotplug.how: When the VM starts, a few free slots (ports) are prepared; each device added while running uses one.
hotplug.caution: If there are none, restart the VM once.

machine.what: (Advanced) The type of virtual motherboard the VM uses.
machine.how: x86_64 nodes use q35, ARM (aarch64) nodes use virt. The VM only runs on nodes of the matching kind.

haPolicy.what: Automatic recovery (HA): if the node fails, this VM is restarted on another node.
haPolicy.how: When the cluster sees a node stop responding, it first cuts that node off (failed-node isolation, fencing), then starts the VM elsewhere — so the same VM never runs twice and corrupts its disk.
haPolicy.caution: The disks must be on a shared pool, or replicated to another node, for the VM to start elsewhere.

ruleViolations.what: Placement rules keep VMs on the same node (together) or on different nodes (apart).
ruleViolations.how: When resources run short or nodes go away, a VM may run without meeting a rule; those rules are listed here.
ruleViolations.when: Bring the node back or free resources and automatic balancing fixes it.

pinned.what: Automatic balancing (the balancer) moves VMs from busy to quiet nodes when the load difference between nodes grows. This VM is excluded.

linkedClone.what: A linked clone uses a template disk as its base and stores only its own changes.
linkedClone.how: It is created in seconds and uses little space, but the base (template) disk must stay.
linkedClone.caution: To delete the template, first flatten these disks (make them independent) or delete the VMs.

cloudInit.what: First-boot setup (cloud-init) puts the host name, account, SSH keys and IP addresses into the guest the first time it boots.
cloudInit.how: Orbivisor attaches a small virtual drive (NoCloud) with the settings, and cloud-init in the guest (cloudbase-init on Windows) reads and applies it.

tpm.what: A TPM is a chip that keeps encryption keys safe; a virtual TPM emulates it for the VM.
tpm.caution: Clearing the TPM state makes disk encryption such as BitLocker ask for its recovery key.

uefiVars.what: A small file where UEFI firmware stores boot entries, Secure Boot keys and similar settings. Created when the VM first boots.

bootOrder.what: The order of devices the VM looks for an OS on when it starts.
bootOrder.how: Devices are tried from the top and the first bootable one is used. A device left out is never booted from.
bootOrder.when: Put the CD-ROM first while installing the OS, and the disk first afterwards (otherwise the installer may start again).
bootOrder.caution: A new order applies from the next start of the VM.

restart.what: Whether Orbivisor starts the VM again on the same node when it stops with an error (for example QEMU crashed).
restart.how:
Never (default): leave it stopped and show the last error.
On failure: start it again after an error stop. A shutdown from inside the guest is not restarted.
restart.when: For VMs that must always run. To start it on another node when its node dies, turn on automatic recovery (HA) instead.

power.what: Whether Orbivisor keeps this VM on or off. It can differ from whether it is running right now (the state).
power.how: The start and stop buttons change it, and after a node reboot or a stop Orbivisor brings the VM back to it.
power.caution: Shutting the OS down inside the guest also sets it to off.

lastError.what: The last error while starting or running the VM.
lastError.how: When Orbivisor cannot start the VM, or the VM stops with an error, the reason stays here. It clears after the next successful start.
lastError.when: Look here first when a VM does not start. The full steps are in the task history.

haError.what: Why automatic recovery (HA) could not restart or move this VM.
haError.how: It is set when a node died and there was no place to start the VM (memory, a 'hard' placement rule, a restricted HA group, no disk replica), or starting failed. It clears when you fix the cause and start the VM again.
haError.when: Look here when an HA VM stayed off.

guestAddresses.what: The addresses the guest's network cards actually use.
guestAddresses.how: Reported by the guest agent (qemu-guest-agent), so addresses changed inside the guest show too. Empty without the agent.
guestAddresses.caution: On SDN networks only the address Orbivisor assigned can talk — if another address shows here, fix the guest's settings.

page.what: A template is a VM frozen as a master copy. Use it to create many VMs with the same OS and settings quickly.
page.how: Deploying makes linked clones that store only their changes on top of the template disk, so it takes seconds. On pools without linked clones the disk is copied in full.
page.when: When downloading an OS image from the image library, turn on 'Make a template after download' to get a template. You can also stop a VM you installed and choose Convert to template.
page.caution: A template with linked clones left can't be deleted or turned back into a VM.

mode.what: How the new VM's disks are made.
mode.how:
Linked clone: shares the template disk and stores only changes — fast and small.
Full copy: an independent disk — slower, but unaffected if the template is deleted.
Linked where possible (default): linked if the pool allows it, otherwise a full copy.
mode.when: Usually the default. Choose full copy for long-lived VMs when you plan to delete the template.

diskSize.what: Disk size of the new VM; empty keeps the template's size.
diskSize.how: The size is what the VM is promised. On thin pools only the data actually written takes space.
diskSize.caution: Disks can only grow, never shrink. Extend the partition inside the guest to use the new space.

maxVcpus.what: (Advanced) How far vCPUs can be raised without turning the VM off.
maxVcpus.how: At start the VM gets this many CPU slots with only the current count switched on. Raising vCPUs later in the editor adds them immediately.
maxVcpus.when: For VMs that must get more CPU without downtime. Usually left empty.
maxVcpus.caution: x86_64 nodes only. A change applies from the next start.

maxMemory.what: (Advanced) How far memory can be raised without turning the VM off.
maxMemory.how: The VM starts with room to grow to this size (virtio-mem); raising memory in the editor adds it immediately.
maxMemory.caution: Linux guests only. A change applies from the next start.

firmware.what: The first program (firmware) that runs when the VM starts.
firmware.how:
UEFI: the default for modern OSes, needed for Secure Boot and TPM (Windows 11).
BIOS: for older OSes or images that boot only with BIOS.
firmware.caution: Changing it after installing the OS may stop the VM from booting.

machine.what: (Advanced) Virtual motherboard type; it decides the chipset and how devices connect.
machine.how: q35: for x86_64 nodes. virt: for ARM (aarch64) nodes. Auto picks the one that fits the node.
machine.when: Rarely changed. The VM runs only on nodes of the chosen kind.

ha.what: Automatic recovery (HA): if the node fails, the VM is restarted on another node.
ha.how: The failed node is cut off first (failed-node isolation, fencing), then the VM starts elsewhere — so it works only on nodes with isolation on.
ha.caution: Disks must be on a shared pool, or replicated, to start on another node.

haState.how:
Started: restarted on another node if its node fails.
Stopped: moved to another node but not started.
Ignored: left out of HA for now (e.g. during maintenance).

haPriority.what: Order of recovery when a failed node takes many VMs down (0–100).
haPriority.example: Database 100, web servers 50 → the database starts first.

pinned.what: Automatic balancing moves VMs to quieter nodes when the load difference between nodes grows. This excludes the VM.
pinned.when: VMs whose licence is tied to a node, or that can't tolerate even a brief pause.

guestWatch.what: Watches whether the guest OS hangs and force-restarts the VM if it stops answering.
guestWatch.how: It asks the guest agent regularly. After a first answer, silence for the set time triggers a restart. During a guest reboot it waits for the agent to answer again.
guestWatch.caution: qemu-guest-agent must be installed and running in the guest. It works only for VMs with automatic recovery (HA) on; after the restart limit the VM is moved to another node.

tpm.what: A virtual TPM chip that keeps encryption keys safe.
tpm.when: Windows 11, BitLocker, or OSes that use measured boot.
tpm.caution: Needs UEFI firmware and swtpm on the node.

secureBoot.what: UEFI feature that boots only signed boot loaders, blocking boot-time malware.
secureBoot.when: Windows 11 and signed Linux distributions (Ubuntu, RHEL family).
secureBoot.caution: Self-built kernels and unsigned OSes won't boot.

guestAgent.what: A channel to a small program in the guest (qemu-guest-agent).
guestAgent.how: With it, the screen shows the guest's IP and OS, shutdowns are clean, and file systems are frozen briefly for consistent snapshots and backups.
guestAgent.when: Recommended for almost every VM. Install qemu-guest-agent in the guest.

cloudInit.what: First-boot setup (cloud-init): puts the host name, account, SSH keys and IP addresses into the guest on its first boot.
cloudInit.how: Orbivisor attaches a small virtual drive (NoCloud, labelled cidata) with the settings; cloud-init in the guest reads and applies it.
cloudInit.when: Cloud images (Ubuntu, Debian, Rocky…) and templates from the image library. Not needed when installing from an ISO.
cloudInit.caution: Changes apply when the VM is restarted.

ciIpMode.what: How this interface gets its address.
ciIpMode.how:
DHCP: automatic from the network's DHCP server (easiest).
Static: you enter the address and gateway below.
SLAAC (IPv6): auto-configured from router adverts.
None: no address of this version.

ciAddress.what: Fixed address and prefix length for the guest.

ciGateway.what: Address of the router used to reach other networks (the internet). Often the subnet's first address (e.g. 10.0.0.1).

ciUserData.how: user-data replaces the #cloud-config built from the fields above (user, password, SSH keys, host name); start it with #cloud-config. Addresses and DNS (network-config) are still built from the fields. vendor-data runs alongside it — use it to add packages or commands.

diskVolume.what: Attaches an existing volume (virtual disk) to this VM.
diskVolume.when: For disks made by a template or import, or detached from another VM.

newVolume.what: Name of a new empty volume (virtual disk). It is blank, so install an OS on it.

diskPool.what: Storage pool for the new disk.
diskPool.how: On a shared pool (NFS, Ceph…) the VM moves quickly and HA can restart it elsewhere. On a local pool the disk is copied in full when moving.

diskSize.what: Size of the new disk in GiB.
diskSize.how: On thin pools the size is only promised; only written data takes space, so the total can exceed the pool (overcommit).
diskSize.caution: You can grow it later but never shrink it. If the pool really fills up, VMs can't write and pause.

diskBus.what: How the disk connects to the VM (virtual device type).
diskBus.how:
virtio-blk: fast virtual device (recommended); works out of the box on Linux and can be added while running.
SATA: compatible; only when there's no VirtIO driver, such as the Windows installer.

nicNetwork.how: Built-in NAT (user) needs no setup but only reaches out; nothing outside can reach the VM. Pick a created network to talk to other VMs and the outside.

nicModel.what: Type of network card the VM sees.
nicModel.how:
virtio: fast virtual device (recommended); works out of the box on Linux.
e1000e: compatible; only without VirtIO drivers, such as during Windows setup.
nicModel.when: For Windows, install the VirtIO drivers after setup and switch to virtio for speed.

nicMac.what: Hardware address of the network card; empty picks one automatically.
nicMac.when: Set it only when a DHCP reservation or licence is tied to a specific MAC.

cdromMedia.what: ISO file to put in this virtual CD/DVD drive.
cdromMedia.when: Insert the installer ISO to install an OS and empty it afterwards. Upload ISOs on the ISO files screen.

replicationNode.what: Another node that keeps a copy of this VM's disks.
replicationNode.how: On each interval only the changes since last time are copied there. If the VM's node fails, HA starts it there from the latest copy.
replicationNode.caution: Changes after the last copy are lost. Use it when you have no shared pool.

replicationMinutes.what: How often, in minutes, the copy is brought up to date.
replicationMinutes.how: Shorter loses less data but uses more disk and network.
replicationMinutes.example: With 15 minutes, up to 15 minutes of changes can be lost if the node fails.

replicationPool.what: Pool on the target node for the copy. By default, the pool with the same name.

schedule.what: Takes snapshots (the disk state at that moment) automatically on a schedule.
schedule.how: Only the configured number of scheduled snapshots is kept, the oldest deleted first. Manual snapshots are untouched.
schedule.when: When you want quick restore points against updates or mistakes. Snapshots live on the same disk, so they don't replace backups.

placement.what: Decides the node the VM runs on.
placement.how: Automatic: when it starts, the server picks a node by free memory, CPU and placement rules. Node: keeps it on that node (pinned, HA and the balancer do not move it either). Failure zone: only nodes in that zone (the zone label).
placement.when: Usually automatic. Pick only for a node or zone with a particular device or license.

flags.what: (Advanced) Hide or add individual CPU features seen by the guest.
flags.when: When a feature makes the guest misbehave or must be hidden for a vulnerability. Usually left empty.
flags.caution: The VM can't move to or start on a node without a feature you turned on.

mode.what: Common CPU baseline for VMs using the cluster model. A shared baseline lets VMs move live between nodes with different CPUs.
mode.how:
Off: like host, the node's CPU as is.
Auto: the best model every node can run (recommended).
Pinned: chosen by hand per architecture.

mask.what: CPU features hidden from every VM.
mask.when: When a CPU vulnerability advisory says to disable a feature.

policy.what: How the vCPUs use the node's physical CPUs.
policy.how:
Shared (default): CPUs are shared with other VMs and can be overcommitted.
Dedicated: each vCPU owns a physical CPU — steady latency, but no other VM can use it.
policy.when: Dedicated only for latency-sensitive VMs (telecom, trading…). The node needs dedicated CPUs set aside first.

threads.what: (Advanced) How the sibling threads (hyper-threading) of a physical core are used.
threads.how:
Siblings first: fill both threads of a core first.
Isolate core: one vCPU per core, sibling left idle (fast, but uses twice the CPUs).
Require siblings: vCPUs placed in sibling pairs.

emulator.what: (Advanced) Where QEMU's own work (I/O and so on) runs, apart from the vCPUs.
emulator.when: For dedicated-CPU VMs, 'Own dedicated CPU' keeps the vCPUs undisturbed.

nodes.what: (Advanced) Large servers split CPUs and memory into cells (NUMA nodes); memory in the same cell is faster. This decides whether the guest sees cells too.
nodes.how: None: one cell. Auto: split when the VM is bigger than one host cell. Manual: you set vCPUs and memory per cell.

hugepages.what: (Advanced) Backs guest memory with large pages (2 MiB or 1 GiB) for faster memory access.
hugepages.how: Memory comes from hugepages the node set aside; that memory can't be used by other VMs.
hugepages.caution: Reserve hugepages in the node's host resources first, or the VM won't start.

listCpus.what: How many vCPU slots this guest NUMA node gets. It must be a multiple of the slots per socket; nodes take sockets in order.

listMemory.what: Memory in MiB for this guest NUMA node. All nodes together must equal the VM's memory.

reserved.what: CPUs kept for the host OS and Orbivisor only; VMs never run there.

dedicated.what: CPUs handed only to VMs with the dedicated policy. The rest (neither reserved nor dedicated) are shared.
dedicated.caution: Leave at least one shared CPU.

hpSize.what: Size of one large page to reserve. 2M is easy; 1G is faster but best reserved at boot.

hpCount.what: Number of pages to reserve; size × count of memory is set aside for VMs.

hpNode.what: Host NUMA node to reserve on. Any lets the kernel spread them.

node.what: Live migration: moves a running VM to another node without stopping it.
node.how: Memory is copied to the target in rounds; at the end the VM pauses very briefly to hand over the rest and continues on the target (the more memory a VM changes, the longer the pause). Shared-pool disks stay; local disks are copied too unless the target already has a replica (then the replica is used).
node.caution: Both nodes need compatible CPU features; nodes you can't pick can't run this VM's CPU.

pool.what: Which pool on the target node receives the copied node-local disks.
pool.caution: Large disks take long, and meanwhile the VM can't be stopped, snapshotted or backed up.

target.what: SDN (virtual) network that receives the VM interfaces.
target.how: Addresses move as they are, so it needs the source's subnet. If none exists, create one with the same subnet.

mode.how:
Auto: stopped VMs as they are, running ones live if possible, otherwise by restarting.
Live: about a one-second interruption.
Restart: stop, switch, start.
Stopped VMs only: running ones are skipped.

page.what: An HA group is the running order for where HA VMs run and where they start again when a node dies.
page.how: Each node in the group gets a priority number. HA places the VM on the live node with the largest number. When a higher node returns, the VM moves back by live migration (unless No failback is on).
page.when: For VMs that should have a usual home and order. If they must run only on certain nodes (licences, GPUs, disks), turn on 'Restricted' — off, they go to other nodes when all group nodes are down.
page.caution: With 'Only on the group's nodes' on, the VM is not started when all those nodes are down.

priority.what: A number that sets the node order (0–1000).
priority.how: Larger goes first. With equal numbers, the node with fewer 'if possible' rule penalties wins, then the less loaded node (with the 'balance' policy), then the one with more free memory.
priority.example: node1=100, node2=50, node3=0 → usually node1; node2 if node1 dies; node3 if both die
priority.when: Leave all at 0 if order does not matter.

page.what: A load balancer has one address clients connect to (VIP) and spreads incoming connections over several member VMs (L4, TCP and UDP).
page.how:
Each listener maps 'VIP port → members'. With health checks on, members that stop answering are taken out and put back when they recover. Turn on the external VIP to reach it from outside through a floating IP (external address).
SDN (OVN) handles it on every node, so no extra appliance or VM is needed.
page.when: When several web or API servers serve one address, and the service must keep running when one fails.
page.caution: The VIP network must be an SDN (overlay) network attached to a router — not an external (provider) network. Members' security groups must accept clients and the health check addresses. There is no HTTP-aware (L7) balancing.

vip.what: The VIP (virtual address) is the load balancer's address clients connect to. It belongs to no VM.
vip.how: It comes from the VIP network's allocation ranges. VMs on other networks of the same router reach it too.
vip.when: Register this address in DNS. Turn on the external VIP for access from outside.

affinity.what: Source affinity (session persistence) sends the same client address to the same member for a set time.
affinity.how: During that time new connections also go to the first member chosen. Empty picks again for every connection.
affinity.when: When the same user must reach the same server, like apps keeping login sessions in server memory.
affinity.caution: Many users behind one NAT can pile onto one member.

listeners.what: A listener is one VIP protocol and port and the members that take it.
listeners.how: A load balancer can have several listeners (up to 16). Members are VM network cards or IPv4 addresses, and the member port may differ from the VIP port.
listeners.caution: A listener without members refuses connections.

health.what: A health check probes each member regularly to see if it is alive.
health.how: Every interval it connects to the member port; no answer within the timeout is a fail. After 'down after' fails in a row the member is out; after 'up after' passes in a row it is back.
health.when: Keep it on. Without it, dead members still get connections.
health.example: interval 5 s, timeout 3 s, up after 2, down after 3 → a dead member is out in about 15 s
health.caution: Checks come from the network's health check address. If members' security groups block it, every member looks down. Members given by IP address instead of VM are not checked and always count as up.

page.what: HA checks rescue VMs from a node that is still alive but cannot reach its switch or storage — half dead.
page.how:
Node ─(checks every 5 s)→ switch and storage. Failing for more than 10 s → this node's VMs start on another node.
If many nodes fail at once, the problem is shared equipment (a switch or NAS), not the node, so it only warns. Only VMs with HA on are moved.
page.when: When nodes use shared storage (NFS, Ceph, iSCSI) or have a single uplink.
page.caution: A node that dies completely is noticed by HA through its heartbeat, even without checks.

role.what: The kind of connection this check looks at. It decides which VMs are affected and the default reaction.
role.how:
Management network: warns by default.
Shared storage connection: VMs with disks on that storage are started again on another node (a VM with stuck disks cannot move while running).
VM network: VMs on that network are moved while running.

kind.how:
Link: whether the network card has a cable link.
Ping: whether the given addresses (such as the gateway or switch) answer.
Pool: reads a small file on the shared pool or checks its paths.
kind.when: Link catches pulled cables; ping sees beyond the switch; pool checks that one shared storage pool is reachable.

onFail.what: What happens when the check fails for longer than the wait time.
onFail.how:
Warn: only tells you.
Live migrate: moves the VMs to another node while running.
Restart elsewhere: stops the VMs and starts them on another node.
Power off the node (force-isolate the failed node): cuts the node off so the same VM never runs twice, then starts the VMs elsewhere.
onFail.caution: Powering off the node also stops its VMs that are not HA.

grace.what: How long (seconds) the check may keep failing before anything happens.
grace.how: Checks run every 5 seconds, so 10 seconds means two failures in a row.
grace.when: If short drops (such as switch restarts) are common, raise it to 30 seconds or more.
grace.example:
10 s (default): fast recovery
60 s: ignores short drops
grace.caution: Longer means VMs come back later in a real failure.

page.what: The topology draws your network layout. It is for looking, not for changing things.
page.how:
At the back: physical (external) networks. Above: routers and their gateway nodes. Below: SDN networks and the VMs on them. On the side: simple networks (bridge, VXLAN). Floating IPs and load balancers sit next to the VMs and networks they point to.
Yellow marks need attention (no gateway, not routed and so on).
page.when: To find where the path breaks when a VM cannot reach the outside, or which networks and routers a VM uses.
page.caution: Things you are not allowed to see are not drawn (only their count is shown).

page.what: A user is one person who signs in to this cluster. Local users (whose passwords the cluster keeps) and every directory (LDAP/OIDC) user who has signed in at least once are listed. Directory users' passwords cannot be changed here; deleting one here also cuts off their sessions and API tokens at once.
page.how:
The global role is the default right across the cluster.
Administrator: everything, including users and settings.
Operator: creates and changes VMs, volumes and backups. Can attach VMs to networks but cannot create or change networks.
Viewer: only looks.
Extra rights per folder or VM are set with roles and groups on the Permissions page.
page.when: Make a separate user for each person. When people share an account, the audit log cannot tell who did what.
