page.caution: Change your own password from the account menu; another administrator changes your role or deletes you.

page.what: An API token is a long secret that programs (scripts, Terraform, Prometheus, orbivisorctl) sign in with instead of a person.
page.how: Send it in the request header Authorization: Bearer <token>. A token without a scope has its creator's rights (the global role plus folder and VM permissions given to them and their groups). With a scope it only has the rights inside that scope (never more than its creator has). It is shown once, when created; the server never shows it again.
page.when: Make a separate token for each automation. If one leaks, delete just that one.
page.caution: A token is as good as a password. Never commit it to a code repository.

page.what: Two-factor sign-in adds one more check, so nobody else can sign in even if your password leaks.
page.how:
Authenticator app: an app such as Google Authenticator shows a 6-digit code that changes every 30 seconds.
Passkey: confirm with a laptop fingerprint, a phone or a security key (YubiKey) — only when you open the UI by domain name.
Recovery codes: emergency codes, each usable once, for when you lose both the app and passkeys.
page.when: Always turn it on for administrator accounts. When the policy requires it, sign-in shows the setup page.
page.caution: Recovery codes are shown only once. Save them somewhere safe, such as a password manager.

page.what: The cluster policy for who must use two-factor sign-in.
page.how: Users with a chosen global role, or in a chosen sign-in realm (local, LDAP), must set up two-factor sign-in at their next sign-in before they get in. OIDC realms are not listed because their sign-in server (IdP) handles it.
page.when: Require it at least for the administrator role.
page.caution: It cannot be turned on until every node runs a version that knows two-factor sign-in.

page.what: Placement rules say whether VMs should be kept together, kept apart, or kept on certain nodes.
page.how: Rules are checked at VM start, migration, HA recovery and balancing. A 'hard' rule never picks a place that breaks it; an 'if possible' rule gives such places a penalty so they are chosen less. But HA recovery may break a rule with 'HA recovery may break this rule' on, and a person can break one with 'Ignore placement rules' in the migrate dialog.
page.example:
Two web VMs on different nodes: 'Different nodes (hard)' + VM label app=web
Databases only on SSD nodes: 'Only on these nodes (hard)' + node label disk=ssd
page.when: With several VMs doing the same job (so one node failure does not take them all), or when VMs need nodes with certain hardware.
page.caution: Too strict 'hard' rules can leave HA no place to start a VM when a node dies — turn on 'HA recovery may break this rule' for such rules.

kind.what: The relation between VMs, or between VMs and nodes.
kind.how:
Same node: keep the VMs on one node together (an app and its database that talk a lot).
Different nodes: keep the VMs on different nodes (two web VMs that must not fail together).
Only these nodes / Not these nodes: tie VMs to nodes or keep them away.
The 'if possible' kinds may be broken when there is no other way.
kind.example:
Two web VMs on different nodes → Different nodes (hard)
Databases only on SSD nodes → Only on these nodes (hard)

weight.what: The importance of an 'if possible' rule (1–100).
weight.how: Each place that breaks the rule gets this many penalty points, and the node with the fewest points is chosen (HA group priority comes first; with equal points, load decides, then free memory).
weight.example: Web spread 80, same rack 20 → when they clash, web spread wins.

page.what: Optimal placement shows the node load and the balancer that evens it out between nodes.
page.how: Nodes send their CPU and memory load every 5 seconds. Every 5 minutes the balancer measures the load difference between nodes and, above the move threshold, works out which VMs to move where. It first moves VMs that break a 'hard' rule to a place that fits, and no move may break a 'hard' rule or add 'if possible' penalties.
page.when: When load piles up on a few nodes. Start with 'Recommend', check the suggestions, then switch to 'Automatic'.
page.caution: Moves are live migrations and use the network while memory is copied.

mode.what: How much the balancer acts by itself.
mode.how:
Off: moves nothing (choosing a node for a VM start still looks at load).
Recommend: only suggests moves; a person presses Apply.
Automatic: makes up to two moves at a time by itself.

policy.how:
Balance: spread load evenly over all nodes.
Pack: VMs being started go to the fullest node that still fits. Running VMs are not gathered, so use Drain node to empty a node. With this policy the balancer only fixes rule violations.

threshold.what: The load difference between nodes (%) at which moves start.
threshold.how: Moves start when the difference is above this and stop below 0.8 times it. A node busier than average by more than twice this is relieved even when the difference is small.
threshold.example:
Threshold 15%, difference now 1.3% → even, no moves
Threshold 15%, difference now 22% → moves suggested
threshold.caution: Too small makes VMs move around often.

page.what: A sign-in realm is where passwords are checked. The local realm is checked by this cluster; LDAP and OIDC realms are checked by your company directory or sign-in service.
page.how: When a user signs in as kim@corp, the corp realm's directory (or IdP) checks them and the groups they belong to set their role. When the company changes their groups, the role changes at the next sign-in. There is no need to create the users first.
page.when: Use it when there are many people, or when sign-in and roles should follow the company directory's accounts and groups. After creating one, press Test to check each step.
page.caution: Deleting or disabling an account in the company directory only blocks new sign-ins. Open sessions (up to 12 hours) and the person's API tokens (they never expire) keep working — to cut them off at once, delete the user on the Users page here (their tokens go with it). Deleting the realm itself stops sign-in, sessions and API tokens of all its users.

kind.how:
LDAP: this cluster connects to the directory server (Active Directory, OpenLDAP) and checks the name and password. Users type their password on the sign-in page.
OIDC: the sign-in button sends the browser to the IdP (Keycloak, Azure AD, Google…), where they sign in and come back. The password never passes through this cluster.
kind.when: LDAP if you only have Active Directory; OIDC if you already use single sign-on.

userFilter.what: The search (LDAP filter) that finds a person in the directory by sign-in name.
userFilter.how: {username} becomes the name the user typed, and one entry matching the filter is looked up under the base DN.
userFilter.example:
Active Directory: (sAMAccountName={username})
OpenLDAP: (uid={username})
Limit to a group: (&(uid={username})(memberOf=cn=opl,ou=groups,dc=example,dc=com))

groups.what: The global role this cluster gives each directory (or IdP) group.
groups.how: At every sign-in the person's groups are read and matched against this table. Matching several gives the highest role (administrator > operator > viewer). Matching none gives the default role.

defaultRole.what: The role for users who match no group.
defaultRole.when: Usually keep None, so only people in the groups you chose get in.
defaultRole.caution: With Viewer, anyone with a company account can see every VM.

page.what: A permission is "to whom · where · which role". For example: the dev-team group · in the dev folder · operator.
page.how: A user's real rights are their global role plus every permission on them (and their groups). A folder permission reaches the VMs, networks, storage and subfolders inside only with 'Apply inside the folder and its subfolders' on — off, it applies to the folder itself only. There are no deny permissions, so to narrow access give a smaller role.
page.when: When global roles are too broad — for example, when each team should handle only the VMs in its own folder.
page.caution: If you remove a permission that gives you access, you cannot add it back yourself.

permissionsPropagate.what: Whether a folder permission passes down.
permissionsPropagate.how:
On: the folder, the folders below it and every VM, network and storage in them.
Off: the folder itself only (for example renaming it) — not even the VMs directly in it.

page.what: A role is a named list of things someone can do.
page.how:
Built-in roles: administrator (everything), operator (manages VMs and volumes), viewer (only looks) — they cannot change.
Custom roles: pick privileges (such as vm.power, vm.snapshot) to make one. Give it to users or groups per folder or VM on the Permissions page.
page.when: When you want to hand out less than a built-in role, such as "only start and stop VMs" or "backups only".
page.caution: A role used by a permission cannot be deleted.

page.what: A group is a set of people you give permissions to.
page.how:
Members: pick local users of this cluster.
Directory groups: link a group of an LDAP or OIDC realm; people in it become members automatically when they sign in.
A permission given to a group goes to every member.
page.when: When two or more people do the same work, make a group and manage their permissions in one place.
page.caution: A group used by a permission cannot be deleted. Remove that permission first.

page.what: The audit log records the requests that change something in this cluster (create, change, delete, sign-in) plus console opens and file-restore downloads. Read-only requests (GET) are not kept. It is where you find who did what when something goes wrong.
page.how: Every node records the requests it receives; this page gathers all nodes' records newest first and names each action in plain words ("Start VM web-01"). Filter by user or part of the address (e.g. /vms/web-01 — everything done to that VM); open a row for the result, IP, time taken and the raw request. Nodes that do not answer are missing.
page.when: To find out why a VM suddenly stopped or a setting changed. For before-and-after values, the change history page is easier.

page.what: A task is one piece of work that takes time to finish, such as starting, moving, backing up or restoring a VM.
page.how: A request creates a task; the node doing it reports progress; at the end it is done, done with a warning, or failed. A failed task shows why in its error line. Tasks that start on their own (HA recovery, scheduled backups) have "automatic" as requester.
page.when: To see what happened after you pressed a button, or why it failed. The Failed filter shows only the problems.

page.what: A folder is a box for VMs (or networks, storage pools). Besides keeping things tidy, it is the unit for permissions and quotas.
page.how:
Permissions: a permission given on a folder with 'Apply inside' passes down to the folders and items below it.
Quotas (VM folders only): caps on vCPUs, memory, disk and VM count for the folder and everything below it. Parent folders' caps apply too. Network and storage folders pass on permissions only.
Moving: drag rows onto a folder on the left, or use Move to folder.
page.when: Make a folder per team or purpose (production/development), give that team permissions on it, and set a quota.
page.caution: Only empty folders can be deleted.

page.what: Change history keeps the before and after of each change to settings such as VMs, networks and rules. By default it keeps up to 100 versions per resource, 365 days and 64 MiB in all; older entries are removed.
page.how: Each row shows who changed it, when and from where (UI, CLI, YAML apply, Terraform, automatic task). Open a row to compare the changed fields side by side and Restore to go back to that value. You can also restore everything to one point in time. Secrets (passwords, tokens) are not recorded, so a restore keeps their current value.
page.when: "It worked yesterday but not today" — find what changed and undo it.
page.caution: History starts when the cluster was upgraded to this version.

page.what: Managing settings as code (YAML) means writing settings in files and applying them all at once. Use it to keep several clusters identical or to review changes in Git.
page.how:
1. Applying files with orbivisorctl apply --set name -f folder creates a set.
2. The cluster remembers the last applied values and compares them with the real values.
3. Any later change (UI, CLI or API) shows as drift; apply again to go back to the file, or accept the current values (then update the files with orbivisorctl export --set).
page.when: When you want settings in Git to review and reproduce. Not needed if you only use the UI.
